blocks.text: Seth woke on the wet rocks. His palms should have been scraped raw. They were not. He touched his face, then his ribs. Everything seemed to be where he had left it.
blocks.alt: Seth pushes himself upright on the wet shore after the impact.

blocks.text: He made it home with a story about slipping near the water. He slept badly. Every time he closed his eyes, the wave returned. In the morning, the bathroom tap snapped off in his hand. Seth stared at it while water sprayed the mirror. “That was loose already,” he told the empty room.

The morning television bulletin reported a flash over Lake Erie and a surge across portions of the lakefront path. Crews were inspecting damaged railings. Officials advised visitors to avoid unstable sections of the shore.

On the bus to school, Seth grabbed the metal seat rail as the driver turned a corner. The tube crumpled beneath his fingers. He kept his hand over the dent until his stop. By lunchtime, he had stopped trying to explain things. After school, he headed back to the lake. He needed somewhere quiet. Somewhere with rocks.
blocks.alt: Seventeen-year-old student Seth accidentally bends a metal seat rail while catching his balance on a Cleveland city bus.

blocks.text: The boulder came up as though it were a cardboard box. Seth’s feet slid. He almost dropped it on his own shoe, then lowered it with a crack that sent a gull into the air.
blocks.alt: Seth awkwardly lifts an impossibly heavy shoreline boulder.

blocks.text: He backed away from the rock. What happened if he grabbed somebody too hard? What if he tried to help and made everything worse?

Seth was heading home when a shout stopped him. The wave had loosened a large tree beside the path. Its roots had finally given way, dropping the trunk across a fisherman’s leg. Two bystanders strained to lift it, but the wood would not budge.

Seth stopped. His hands curled inside his sleeves. He could walk away and find someone who knew what they were doing. Then the fisherman tried to shift and cried out. Seth crossed the path. “Let me try.”

A slim blonde woman in a white blouse and pink skirt reached the gathering crowd with her notebook already in hand. She looked to be in her early twenties, with a freckled face and an intent expression. Her hair was windblown, but she watched the boy lifting the trunk more closely than the people shouting around him.
Seth slid both hands beneath the trunk and lifted. He held it steady while the helpers pulled the fisherman clear.
blocks.alt: Seth lifts a fallen tree as two bystanders pull a fisherman clear; a young woman with a notebook watches with impressed curiosity.

blocks.text: He lowered the tree onto the empty path with a heavy thud. The fisherman caught his sleeve. “You saved my life! That thing would’ve crushed me. What’s your name, kid?”
“Seth Zerdowski.” He glanced at the tree as though someone else might have lifted it. “Glad you’re all right.”
“Zerdowski? Super Zerdo, I’d say!” the fisherman said. One of the helpers laughed and repeated it. The young woman with the notebook wrote the name down.

A little warmth spread across Seth’s shoulders, although the lake wind still tugged at his sleeves. He rubbed the back of his neck. Probably the effort. By the time he turned toward the woman with the notebook, it had passed.
“I’m Jenny Jenkins, a junior reporter for the Defender.” Her green eyes went from Seth to the tree. He suddenly forgot what to do with his hands. “Have you been able to lift trees for long?”
“N-not really. Since—well, yesterday, I think.” Seth caught his heel on a root and steadied himself. Lifting the tree had been easier than answering her.

Jenny’s pen stopped at yesterday. “Were you here when the wave came in?” “It hit me,” Seth said. “This morning I broke the tap. Then the rail on the bus. I don’t know what happened to me.” She studied him before writing that down.

blocks.alt: Daniel crouches behind shoreline bushes with an analog meter, secretly listening to Seth and Jenny beside the fallen tree.
blocks.text: Beyond the path, Daniel crouched behind the bushes with a portable meter. He had spent the day taking readings along the lake, trying to trace the light he had seen. He reached the bushes as the reporter asked how long the boy had been able to lift trees. Now he heard about the wave, the broken tap, and the bus rail. He looked from the boy to the needle on his meter, then slipped away while they were still talking.

Jenny smiled and asked to speak again. Seth agreed a little too quickly and gave her his home telephone number. Then he slipped away while she checked on the fisherman. She watched him go before returning to her notes.
At home, Seth tested the front door with two fingers before closing it. He had helped somebody. For once, he had done something right.
That evening, Daniel wrote beside the lake readings: STRENGTH AFTER EXPOSURE. He had come to measure what was in the water. Now he wanted to collect it.
